# Research notes on 1 Kings 9, verse by verse

**Gaps.** I ran out of searches and page fetches before I could check the Catholic and Orthodox sites (newadvent.org, catholic.com, oca.org), bibleodyssey.org, or any prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace teaching. Nothing from those appears below. The only Catholic voice is Haydock's commentary on StudyLight. Several of the Wesleyan voices (Wesley, Benson, Clarke) are quoted on StudyLight pages, not on wesley.nnu.edu or seedbed.com. The Enduring Word and Pulpit Commentary pages I fetched were cut off partway, so I have Pulpit's verse notes only for vv. 1–9; its vv. 10–28 notes come from search snippets.

---

## 1. Traditional reading

**v. 1**
- Guzik notes this was about 24 years into Solomon's reign. Now he had to live after finishing his greatest work. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-9/
- John Trapp, quoted by both Guzik and Precept Austin: the word "desired" is the longing of a young man for his bride. Trapp thinks this shows Solomon loved his buildings too much and "here began his fall." https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-kings-9-commentary
- J. R. Miller (on Precept Austin) says busy work had protected Solomon. Free time, fame and luxury once the projects were done became his time of danger. https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-kings-9-commentary
- Pulpit Commentary thinks this vision probably came about 13 years after the dedication, not right after it. Its reason is that the answer sounds threatening, as if Solomon was already starting to drift. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/1-kings-9.html

**v. 2**
- Pulpit: like Gibeon, this appearance was in a dream (1 Kings 3:5). https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/1-kings-9.html
- Guzik quotes Spurgeon urging older believers to seek a fresh visit from God, a "second visitation." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-9/

**v. 3**
- Guzik: Solomon built the house, but only God could make it holy. He quotes F. B. Meyer: "Man builds; God hallows." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-9/
- Pulpit: Solomon had asked that God's eyes be open toward the house. God gives more: His eyes and His heart will be there. The eye watches over it, and the heart cherishes it. The temple's later ruin was caused by the nation turning from God. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/1-kings-9.html

**v. 4**
- Pulpit: David was not perfect. His "integrity" was his steady loyalty to the true God, with no flirting with idols even when he sinned badly. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/1-kings-9.html
- Guzik: God did not demand perfect obedience. Walking as David walked was within Solomon's reach. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-9/

**v. 5**
- Pulpit: this answers Solomon's prayer in 8:26 and echoes 2 Samuel 7. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/1-kings-9.html
- Precept Austin: the promise depends on the stated conditions. God turns down Solomon's request in 8:25–26 for a guarantee. https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-kings-9-commentary

**v. 6**
- Pulpit: the Hebrew ("if turning, you turn") means complete, not partial, turning away. Like God's promises, His warnings reach to the children too. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/1-kings-9.html

**v. 7**
- Pulpit: the wording matches Deuteronomy 28:37. It was fulfilled in 2 Kings 25. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/1-kings-9.html
- Guzik: God's answer was not a promise to bless the temple whatever happened. Israel would be tempted to make an idol of the temple itself. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-9/

**v. 8**
- Pulpit: the Hebrew literally says "this house shall be high," probably meaning it will stand out as a warning example. Some ancient translations read "destroyed" instead. The "hissing" is mockery, not fear. Pulpit adds that the wording sounds like Jeremiah, which suggests the writer kept the main ideas of the dream rather than its exact words. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/1-kings-9.html

**v. 9**
- Pulpit: this verse is based on Deuteronomy 29:25. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/1-kings-9.html
- Coffman: Jeremiah (26:18) and Micah (3:12) later prophesied the same exile and destruction. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/1-kings-9.html
- Caution: Pulpit's sermon notes on vv. 1–9 apply these verses to the later history of the Jewish people in language that is harsh and antisemitic by today's standards. Use with care. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/1-kings-9.html

**v. 10**
- Pulpit: vv. 10–28 show the resources behind Solomon's projects: his alliance with Hiram and the forced labour of subject peoples. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/1-kings-9.html
- Wiseman (quoted by Precept Austin) lists three sources of funding: Hiram, forced labour, and sea trade. https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-kings-9-commentary

**v. 11**
- Wesley: these towns lay inside the wider borders God promised (Genesis 15:18) but outside the land divided by lot in Joshua's day. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/1-kings-9.html
- Pulpit: they were really just villages. Grand names for small gifts were an Eastern habit. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/1-kings-9.html

**vv. 12–13 (Cabul)**
- Josephus says "Cabul" is a Phoenician word meaning "displeasing" (Barnes, Henry). https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-kings/9-13.html
- Constable: it sounds like the Hebrew for "good for nothing," because the area was not productive. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-kings/9-13.html
- Clarke (Methodist) says the scholars do not agree on the meaning. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-kings/9-13.html
- Haydock (Catholic): kings called each other "brother"; Solomon and Hiram always got on well. The word means "dirty or displeasing," though the real meaning is uncertain. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-kings/9-13.html
- Keil: the towns were mostly heathen and probably run down. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_kings/9-13.htm
- Pulpit: Hiram wanted farmland for grain, not more coastline. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/1-kings-9.html
- 2 Chronicles 8:2 suggests the towns were given back and Solomon resettled them with Israelites (Barnes; Keil). https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-kings/9-13.html

**v. 14**
- Wesley and Benson read it as "Hiram *had* sent." So large a sum explains why Hiram felt short-changed. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/1-kings-9.html
- MacArthur: about 4.5 tons of gold, with the towns given in exchange. https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-kings-9-commentary
- Jamieson-Fausset-Brown mentions Josephus's story that the gold may have been forfeits from a riddle contest between the two kings. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_kings/9-13.htm

**v. 15**
- Wesley: the "levy" was of men and of money, raised to repay Hiram and to fund the building. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/1-kings-9.html
- Guzik: the "Millo" was probably a fortress, or terracing on the slope of the City of David. Quoting Patterson and Austel, he says Hazor, Megiddo and Gezer have gate complexes from Solomon's era that are nearly identical. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-9/
- Bible Hub's notes link the Millo to large stepped stone supports found in Jerusalem. https://biblehub.com/1_kings/9.htm

**v. 16**
- Patterson and Austel (quoted by Guzik): Gezer had been a strong Canaanite city that Israel did not hold until Solomon. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-9/
- Bible Hub: Egyptian destruction layers under Solomon's Gezer fit Pharaoh's burning of the city. https://biblehub.com/1_kings/9.htm

**vv. 17–19**
- Guzik's NKJV text reads "Tadmor" where the BSB has "Tamar." 2 Chronicles 8:4–6 (quoted by Precept Austin) also names Tadmor, Beth-horon and the store cities. https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-kings-9-commentary

**vv. 20–21**
- Guzik: this was another compromise. God had commanded that these peoples be driven out, not used as slave labour. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-9/
- Precept Austin cites Deuteronomy 7:1–2 alongside this. https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-kings-9-commentary

**vv. 22–23**
- Precept Austin: this does not contradict 5:13. Solomon drafted Israelites for temple work, which later caused trouble, but he made no Israelite a slave. https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-kings-9-commentary

**v. 24**
- Jamieson-Fausset-Brown: vv. 24–25 round off the building record. They show Solomon fixing problems from the start of his reign (3:1–4). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_kings/9-25.htm
- Pulpit: v. 24 looks back to 3:1. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_kings/9-25.htm

**v. 25**
- Most commentators say "three times" means the three pilgrim feasts: Passover, Weeks and Tabernacles (Ellicott, Gill, Poole). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_kings/9-25.htm
- Gill: Solomon did not burn incense himself, since no king could (compare Uzziah). "Finished the house" means its worship was now fully running. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_kings/9-25.htm
- Pulpit: the verse may show there was no more offering at the high places (looking back to 3:2). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_kings/9-25.htm

**vv. 26–27**
- Pulpit: Israel had no fleet and little sea experience, so Hiram probably supplied the materials and had the ships built. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/1-kings-9.html
- Barnes: the Ophir trade was probably already running, in Phoenician or Egyptian hands, when Solomon joined it. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-kings/9-27.html
- Wesley: Hiram's ships may have come from a Tyrian colony on a Red Sea island (citing Strabo). https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/1-kings-9.html
- Despite the Cabul episode, Hiram kept working with Solomon. Hiram gave the seamanship, and Solomon gave access to the Red Sea. https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-kings-9-commentary

**v. 28**
- Wesley: Chronicles says 450 talents. Perhaps 30 went to Hiram's men, leaving 420 for the king. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/1-kings-9.html
- Pulpit explains the difference as a copying confusion between Hebrew number letters. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/1-kings-9.html
- Chuck Smith (Calvary Chapel) thinks the fleet went to Africa. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-kings/9-25.html
- Another entry on the same StudyLight page suggests the East Indies, possibly Ceylon. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-kings/9-27.html

## 2. Where Protestant traditions differ

**vv. 4–7: Is the promise to David's line conditional?**
- **Reformed (Ligonier):** the covenant is "unconditional" in that God would make sure David had the obedient son it required, by sending Christ. How much the other kings enjoyed its blessings depended on their good-faith obedience and repentance. https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/guidance-to-solomon
- **Schreiner (monergism.com):** nearly all biblical covenants have both conditional and unconditional parts. The covenant with David is ultimately unconditional and is fulfilled in Jesus as the obedient king. https://www.monergism.com/10-things-you-should-know-about-biblical-covenants
- **Dispensational (bible.org, Walvoord):** the promise is unconditional. Solomon's line was cut off from the throne, but David's line and its right to rule are never lost. https://bible.org/seriespage/eschatological-problems-vii-fulfillment-davidic-covenant
- **GotQuestions** also calls it unconditional. https://www.gotquestions.org/Davidic-covenant.html
- **Middle view (Precept Austin, quoting Paul House):** God keeps the eternal side of the covenant, through Christ. The temporary side, about Solomon and his sons, depends on obedience. https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-kings-9-commentary
- **Restoration Movement (Coffman, on Psalm 132):** a similar split. The promise of the Messiah is unconditional; keeping the political dynasty on the throne is conditional. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/132-14.html

**vv. 11–14: Did Solomon treat Hiram fairly?** This split is between individual teachers, not denominations.
- **Puritan and Methodist voices defend Solomon.** Matthew Henry thinks neither king behaved badly. The land was good, but merchant Tyrians had no use for farmland. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/1Ki/1Ki_009.cfm
- Wesley and Benson agree, and say Solomon surely gave Hiram something else he liked better. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/1-kings-9.html
- **Modern evangelicals are more critical.** Paul House sees a "conniving" side of Solomon. Dale Ralph Davis calls it no way to treat a generous friend. https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-kings-9-commentary
- Guzik (Calvary Chapel) says giving away Israel's God-given land was wrong. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-9/

## 3. Other views

**v. 8:** Pulpit mentions Thenius's proposed change of the Hebrew to "ruins." Pulpit rejects it because no manuscript or ancient translation supports it. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/1-kings-9.html

**v. 13:** Keil thinks "Cabul" may mean "pledged land." On this view the gold was a loan secured by the towns, and the towns came back once the loan was repaid. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/1-kings-9.html

**v. 25: Did Solomon act as a priest?**
- The Cambridge Bible notes that some scholars think Solomon did the priestly acts himself. That would mean the Levites' exclusive role came later. It also notes that the Vatican manuscript of the Greek Old Testament omits vv. 15–25. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_kings/9-25.htm
- Dean Stanley claimed Solomon himself entered the Holy Place to burn incense. Pulpit says this has no basis in the text. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_kings/9-25.htm
- Barnes, Gill and Henry say the priests did it for him: people are said to do what they cause to be done. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-kings/9-25.html
- Guzik leaves both options open. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-9/

**v. 28: Where was Ophir?** The NET Bible's glossary says the site is uncertain: southern or southeastern Arabia, or East or South Africa. https://classic.net.bible.org/dictionary.php?word=ophir

**On the theme of wealth:** I found no prosperity-teaching sources. Two older voices warn against prosperity. Pulpit calls riches "third-rate blessings." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/1-kings-9.html J. R. Miller says people need God's grace most when life is going well. https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-kings-9-commentary
